items.title: Derived series and solvable Lie algebras
items.statement: For a Lie algebra g, set g^(0)=g and g^(r+1)=[g^(r),g^(r)]. The algebra is solvable when g^(m)=0 for some m.
items.strategy: Define [a,a] as the span of brackets and verify inductively that every term is an ideal; no finite-dimensional or field restriction is used.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §3.1–3.2

items.title: Derived-series terms are characteristic ideals
items.statement: Every automorphism of g preserves each term g^(r) of the derived series.
items.strategy: Use f([a,a])=[f(a),f(a)] and induction, applying the same inclusion to f inverse for equality; ideality follows simultaneously from Jacobi.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §3, Generalities

items.title: Solvable length
items.statement: For solvable g, its derived length is the least m with g^(m)=0; the zero algebra has length zero.
items.strategy: Use well-ordering of the nonempty subset of natural numbers where the derived series vanishes.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §3.1–3.2

items.title: Lower central series and nilpotent Lie algebras
items.statement: Set gamma_1(g)=g and gamma_(r+1)(g)=[g,gamma_r(g)]. The algebra is nilpotent when gamma_(c+1)(g)=0 for some c.
items.strategy: Define brackets of subspaces by linear span and use Jacobi inductively to establish ideality of every gamma_r.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2.1–2.2

items.title: Lower-central-series terms are characteristic ideals
items.statement: Every automorphism of g preserves every gamma_r(g).
items.strategy: Induct from f(g)=g and f([g,gamma_r])=[g,f(gamma_r)]; apply f inverse for equality.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Ch. I §6

items.title: Nilpotency class
items.statement: For nonzero nilpotent g, its nilpotency class is the least c>=1 with gamma_(c+1)(g)=0; the zero algebra has class zero.
items.strategy: Use the least vanishing lower-central index and state the zero convention separately.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2.1–2.2

items.title: Upper central series
items.statement: Set Z_0(g)=0 and define Z_(r+1)(g) by Z_(r+1)(g)/Z_r(g)=Z(g/Z_r(g)); the next theorem proves inductively that these are ideals and characterizes termination.
items.strategy: Take the inverse image of the quotient center under the canonical projection; representative independence comes from the published quotient bracket.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §5.4

items.title: Lower and upper central series characterize nilpotence
items.statement: For g and c>=0, gamma_(c+1)(g)=0 iff Z_c(g)=g. Consequently the lower series terminates iff the upper series reaches g.
items.strategy: Translate both conditions into existence of a central filtration of length c. For one direction use gamma_i subset a_i inductively; for the other use [g,Z_i] subset Z_(i-1) and reverse the upper filtration.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2.1–2.2

items.title: Nilpotent Lie algebras are solvable
items.statement: For every r>=0, g^(r) is contained in gamma_(2^r)(g); hence every nilpotent Lie algebra is solvable.
items.strategy: Prove [gamma_p,gamma_q] subset gamma_(p+q) by Jacobi induction, then induct on r and use vanishing of the lower series.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §5.4

items.title: Subalgebras, quotients, and extensions of solvable Lie algebras
items.statement: Subalgebras and quotients of solvable Lie algebras are solvable. If i is a solvable ideal and g/i is solvable, then g is solvable, with dl(g)<=dl(i)+dl(g/i).
items.strategy: Compare derived series under inclusion and quotient. If the quotient has length m, g^(m) lies in i, and n additional derived steps vanish when i has length n.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Proposition 3.4

items.title: Subalgebras, quotients, and finite products of nilpotent Lie algebras
items.statement: Subalgebras and quotients of nilpotent Lie algebras are nilpotent. A nonempty finite direct product is nilpotent of class the maximum of the factor classes; the empty product is the zero Lie algebra and has class zero.
items.strategy: Compare lower central series under inclusion and quotient, and compute the lower series of a finite product componentwise. Treat the empty product separately and do not assert closure under arbitrary extensions.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Proposition 2.5

items.title: A central extension of a nilpotent Lie algebra is nilpotent
items.statement: If i is contained in Z(g) and g/i is nilpotent of class c, then g is nilpotent of class at most c+1.
items.strategy: Pull the quotient central filtration back to g and append i then 0, or observe gamma_(c+1)(g) subset i and bracket once more with g.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Proposition 2.5(b)

items.title: A nonzero nilpotent Lie algebra has nonzero center
items.statement: If g is nonzero and nilpotent, then Z(g) is nonzero.
items.strategy: Take the last nonzero lower-central term; its bracket with g is the next, zero term, so it lies in the center.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Proposition 2.5(c)

items.title: Nilpotent transformations and nil representations
items.statement: An endomorphism T is nilpotent if T^m=0 for some m. A representation rho:g→gl(V) is nil when rho(x) is nilpotent for every x in g.
items.strategy: Keep operator nilpotence distinct from nilpotence of the image Lie algebra and from nilpotence of the abstract source algebra.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2, Engel's theorem

items.title: Engel's common-zero-vector lemma
items.statement: If V is nonzero finite-dimensional over any field and g is a Lie subalgebra of gl(V) all of whose elements are nilpotent, then some nonzero v satisfies xv=0 for every x in g.
items.strategy: Induct on dim g. For a maximal proper subalgebra h, each ad_H on g is nilpotent because H is nilpotent on V and ad_H=L_H-R_H on End(V); induction applied to h on g/h yields a nonzero normalized coset, so maximality makes h an ideal of codimension one. Induction also makes the common h-kernel in V nonzero; ideality makes it stable under a complement x, whose nilpotence supplies a nonzero vector killed by all of g.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 2.8 and proof

items.title: Engel triangularization theorem
items.statement: Under the hypotheses of the common-zero-vector lemma, V has a flag whose successive quotients are annihilated by g; equivalently every rho(x) is strictly upper triangular in one basis.
items.strategy: Induct on dim V: take the common zero line, descend the nil action to the quotient, triangularize there, and lift a quotient basis.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 1.35

items.title: Engel's theorem
items.statement: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra over any field is nilpotent iff ad_x is nilpotent for every x.
items.strategy: One direction follows from iterated commutators in the lower series. Conversely apply Engel triangularization to ad(g), obtaining a basis with [g,V_i] contained in V_(i-1), hence a terminating central filtration.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Corollary 2.11

items.title: Nilpotent adjoint action yields a central series
items.statement: If every ad_x is nilpotent on finite-dimensional g, then g admits a finite filtration g=a_0⊃...⊃a_m=0 with [g,a_i]⊆a_(i+1), and its upper central series reaches g.
items.strategy: Read the invariant flag supplied by Engel for the adjoint representation as the required central filtration, then apply the upper/lower characterization.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 2.8 and Corollary 2.11

items.title: Codimension-one ideals in nilpotent Lie algebras
items.statement: If h is a proper subalgebra of a finite-dimensional nilpotent g, then h is contained in an ideal of g of codimension one.
items.strategy: Induct on dim g using a nonzero central line kz. If z lies in h, quotient by kz and pull back the inductively obtained hyperplane ideal. If z does not lie in h and h+kz is all of g, then h is already a codimension-one ideal; otherwise apply induction to the proper subalgebra (h+kz)/kz of g/kz and pull back.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Propositions 2.5–2.6

items.title: Codimension-one ideal in a nonzero solvable Lie algebra
items.statement: A nonzero finite-dimensional solvable Lie algebra over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field has an ideal of codimension one.
items.strategy: Solvability gives [g,g] proper. Choose a hyperplane in the nonzero abelianization g/[g,g] and pull it back; its inverse image is an ideal. The stated hypotheses are retained although this elementary step works over any field.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Proposition 1.23

items.title: Lie's theorem
items.statement: Let g be finite-dimensional solvable over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero and let V be a nonzero finite-dimensional g-module. Then V contains a common eigenvector for g.
items.strategy: Induct on dim g using a codimension-one ideal h. Start with an h-weight vector, span its iterates under a complement x, prove h acts there by the same weight using the commutator-trace identity and characteristic zero, and take an x-eigenvector in that stable space.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 1.25

items.title: Simultaneous triangularization of solvable representations
items.statement: Under Lie's theorem hypotheses, V has a complete invariant flag, equivalently a basis in which every rho(x) is upper triangular.
items.strategy: Induct on dim V using the common eigenline, the quotient representation, and lifted quotient basis vectors.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 3.7

items.title: Irreducible representations of solvable complex Lie algebras are one-dimensional
items.statement: Every nonzero finite-dimensional irreducible complex representation of a finite-dimensional solvable complex Lie algebra has dimension one.
items.strategy: Lie's theorem produces an invariant eigenline; irreducibility forces that line to equal the whole module.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Theorem 5.24

items.title: Derived algebra of a solvable linear Lie algebra is nilpotent
items.statement: Over an algebraically closed characteristic-zero field, if g is a finite-dimensional solvable subalgebra of gl(V), then [g,g] consists of nilpotent endomorphisms and is a nilpotent Lie algebra.
items.strategy: Triangularize g simultaneously; commutators are strictly upper triangular, hence nilpotent operators. Apply Engel's theorem to the derived subalgebra.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Corollary 3.8

items.title: The derived algebra of a solvable Lie algebra is nilpotent in characteristic zero
items.statement: For any characteristic-zero field, the derived algebra of a finite-dimensional solvable Lie algebra is nilpotent.
items.strategy: To remain in ZF, choose a finite basis and descend the structure constants to the finitely generated prime subfield k0; this countable field has a deterministically constructed algebraic closure. Derived and lower central series commute with scalar extension, so solvability descends to g0. Over the algebraic closure apply the linear theorem to ad(g0); its kernel on the derived algebra is central, so lift nilpotence through that kernel, descend the vanishing lower series to g0, and extend back to k.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Proposition 1.39

items.title: Solvability criterion via the derived algebra
items.statement: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field is solvable iff its derived algebra is nilpotent.
items.strategy: The forward implication is the preceding corollary. Conversely [g,g] nilpotent implies it solvable, while g/[g,g] is abelian; apply extension closure.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Corollary 3.8

items.title: Solvable radical
items.statement: For finite-dimensional g, rad(g) is its largest solvable ideal; existence and uniqueness are supplied by the next theorem.
items.strategy: Define the intended universal property, with well-definedness explicitly deferred to the cited justification theorem.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Corollary 3.5 and Definition 3.6

items.title: The sum of solvable ideals is solvable
items.statement: The sum of two solvable ideals is a solvable ideal. Hence a finite-dimensional Lie algebra has a unique largest solvable ideal, the sum of all its solvable ideals.
items.strategy: For ideals i,j, use (i+j)/i congruent to j/(i intersect j) and extension closure. Finite dimensionality lets the sum of all ideals be generated by finitely many of them, avoiding any choice or infinite-extension claim.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Corollary 3.5

items.title: The radical is characteristic and its quotient is semisimple
items.statement: Every automorphism preserves rad(g), and rad(g/rad(g))=0.
items.strategy: Automorphisms carry solvable ideals to solvable ideals, so maximality gives equality. A solvable ideal of the quotient has a solvable inverse image by extension closure, hence must be zero.

references.title: Etingof, Introduction to Representation Theory / Lie notes, Proposition 14.6

items.title: Nilradical
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional characteristic-zero Lie algebra g, nilrad(g) is its largest nilpotent ideal; existence and characteristicity are supplied next.
items.strategy: State the universal property without identifying it with the generally non-linear set of ad-nilpotent elements.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Corollary 2.24

items.title: Existence and characteristicity of the nilradical in characteristic zero
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional characteristic-zero Lie algebra has a unique largest nilpotent ideal, and this ideal is characteristic.
items.strategy: The sum of two nilpotent ideals is solvable. After scalar extension, Lie triangularization applies to its adjoint action on g; every element of either ideal is ad-nilpotent because its first bracket lands in that ideal, so both have zero diagonal and their sum acts strictly upper triangular. Engel makes the sum nilpotent. Finite dimensionality reduces the sum of all nilpotent ideals to a finite sum; uniqueness makes it automorphism-invariant.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Proposition 1.40 and Corollary 1.41

items.title: The commutator with the radical lies in the nilradical
items.statement: For finite-dimensional g over a characteristic-zero field, [g,rad(g)] is contained in nilrad(g).
items.strategy: First prove that if s is solvable and D is a derivation, then D(s) lies in nilrad(s): the semidirect product kt semidirect_D s is solvable, its derived algebra is nilpotent, and D(s)=[t,s] lies there. Apply this to each inner derivation restricted to r=rad(g), obtaining [g,r] inside nilrad(r). The same containment makes nilrad(r) a nilpotent ideal of g; maximality in both directions identifies nilrad(r)=nilrad(g).

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Proposition 1.40 and Corollary 1.41

items.title: The derived algebra of the radical lies in the nilradical
items.statement: [rad(g),rad(g)] is contained in nilrad(g).
items.strategy: Use rad(g) subset g in the first bracket entry of the preceding containment.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 6.9

items.title: Derivations preserve the nilradical in characteristic zero
items.statement: If D is a derivation of a finite-dimensional characteristic-zero Lie algebra g, then D(nilrad(g)) is contained in nilrad(g).
items.strategy: Let I=nilrad(g) and J=I+D(I). Use the generalized Leibniz formula for iterated brackets and the characteristic-zero combinatorial argument of Maksimenko: if I has class c, repeated differentiation forces sufficiently long brackets in J into successively deeper powers I^m and ultimately to zero. Thus J is a nilpotent ideal; maximality of I gives D(I) subset I. Treat I=0 separately and identify exactly where factorial coefficients are inverted.

references.title: Maksimenko, On action of outer derivations on nilpotent ideals of Lie algebras, Theorem 1 and Lemmas 1–5, pp. 74–82

items.title: Semisimple Lie algebras
items.statement: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra is semisimple when its solvable radical is zero.
items.strategy: Use the radical definition, allowing the zero Lie algebra to be semisimple under this convention.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Definition 4.2

items.title: Reductive Lie algebras
items.statement: Over characteristic zero, a finite-dimensional Lie algebra is reductive when g=Z(g)⊕[g,g] with [g,g] semisimple. Equivalence with the other standard characterizations is deferred to the next A page.
items.strategy: Record the direct-sum convention explicitly and avoid using the later equivalence as well-definedness here.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §6.1

items.title: Every solvable Lie algebra is nilpotent
items.statement: False: solvability does not imply nilpotence.
items.strategy: Refute with the two-dimensional affine Lie algebra [x,y]=y: its derived series stops after ky, while every lower-central term after the first equals ky.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, introductory examples before §2

items.title: Nilpotent-by-nilpotent extensions are always nilpotent
items.statement: False: an extension with nilpotent ideal and nilpotent quotient need not be nilpotent.
items.strategy: Use the affine algebra ky triangleleft g with abelian ideal and quotient but [g,ky]=ky forever.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Aside 2.3

items.title: A nilpotent acting basis suffices for Engel's theorem
items.statement: False: nilpotence of ad_x only for the members of one vector-space basis does not imply nilpotence of every ad_x.
items.strategy: In sl_2 use the basis e, f, and h+e-f. Each of these three matrices is nilpotent, hence ad-nilpotent, but their span is all of sl_2 and contains h, whose adjoint has eigenvalues 0,2,-2.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, §6 warning around Engel's theorem

items.title: Lie's theorem is field- and characteristic-free
items.statement: False: Lie's theorem can fail over non-algebraically-closed fields and in positive characteristic.
items.strategy: Use a real rotation representation for the field obstruction and the standard characteristic-p cyclic module for [x,y]=y for the characteristic obstruction.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Remark 13.2

items.title: Every irreducible real representation of a solvable Lie algebra is one-dimensional
items.statement: False: the one-dimensional abelian real Lie algebra has irreducible real representations of dimension two.
items.strategy: Let its generator act by the rotation matrix with minimal polynomial t^2+1; no real invariant line exists.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, §5 field warning

items.title: The nilradical is the set of all ad-nilpotent elements
items.statement: False in general: the set of ad-nilpotent elements need not be a linear subspace, whereas the nilradical is the largest nilpotent ideal.
items.strategy: In sl_2, e and f are ad-nilpotent but e+f is semisimple and not ad-nilpotent; semisimplicity also makes the nilradical zero.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2.13 and Corollary 2.24

title: Solvable and Nilpotent Lie Algebras — Examples

items.title: Abelian Lie algebras are nilpotent of class one
items.statement: Every nonzero abelian Lie algebra has gamma_2=0 and nilpotency class one; the zero algebra has class zero.
items.strategy: Compute the lower central series directly and retain the zero convention.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2.1

items.title: The Heisenberg Lie algebra is two-step nilpotent
items.statement: For the three-dimensional algebra with [x,y]=z and z central, gamma_2=kz and gamma_3=0, so the class is two.
items.strategy: Evaluate all basis brackets and both nontrivial lower-central terms.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, introductory Heisenberg example

items.title: Strictly upper triangular matrices form a nilpotent Lie algebra
items.statement: The Lie algebra n_n of strictly upper triangular n-by-n matrices is nilpotent; its lower series moves at least one superdiagonal at each bracket and has class n-1 for n>=2.
items.strategy: Filter by the minimum superdiagonal and use [F_p,F_q] subset F_(p+q), checking a chain of matrix units gives sharpness.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §2.1

items.title: Upper triangular matrices are solvable but not nilpotent
items.statement: For n>=2 the upper triangular matrix Lie algebra b_n is solvable and not nilpotent.
items.strategy: Its first derived algebra lies in the strictly upper triangular algebra, so the derived series terminates; a diagonal matrix repeatedly brackets a matrix unit to a nonzero scalar multiple, so the lower series does not terminate.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §§2–3 examples

items.title: The two-dimensional affine Lie algebra is solvable, not nilpotent
items.statement: For g=kx⊕ky with [x,y]=y, g^(1)=ky and g^(2)=0, while gamma_r=ky for all r>=2.
items.strategy: Compute both series on the displayed basis.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, introductory affine example

items.title: The plane Euclidean-motion Lie algebra is solvable
items.statement: The Lie algebra e(2)=so(2)⋉R^2 has derived algebra R^2 and second derived algebra zero, hence derived length two; it is not nilpotent.
items.strategy: Use the standard infinitesimal rotation action, whose image spans the translation ideal, and show lower commutators with the rotation generator never vanish.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §5.4 examples

items.title: Series of a standard filiform Lie algebra
items.statement: For n>=3, the Lie algebra with basis e_1,...,e_n, brackets [e_1,e_i]=e_(i+1) for 2<=i<n, and all other basis brackets zero has gamma_r=span(e_(r+1),...,e_n) for 2<=r<=n-1, nilpotency class n-1, and derived length two.
items.strategy: Induct on r for the lower series and calculate that the derived algebra span(e_3,...,e_n) is abelian.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §5.4

items.title: Radical and nilradical of the affine Lie algebra
items.statement: For [x,y]=y in characteristic zero, rad(g)=g and nilrad(g)=ky.
items.strategy: Solvability makes the whole algebra the radical. The ideal ky is abelian, while any ideal containing an element with nonzero x-component is all of g and hence not nilpotent.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, remarks after Proposition 1.40

items.title: A nilpotent-by-nilpotent extension need not be nilpotent
items.statement: The affine algebra has abelian ideal ky and abelian quotient g/ky, but is not nilpotent.
items.strategy: Display the short exact sequence and reuse the explicit persistent lower-central calculation.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Aside 2.3

items.title: A two-dimensional irreducible real representation of an abelian Lie algebra
items.statement: Let the generator of the one-dimensional abelian real Lie algebra act on R^2 by J=[[0,-1],[1,0]]. This representation is irreducible over R.
items.strategy: Any invariant real line would give a real eigenvector of J, but its characteristic polynomial t^2+1 has no real root.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, §5 field warning

items.title: Positive-characteristic failure of Lie's theorem
items.statement: In characteristic p, the solvable algebra [x,y]=y has a p-dimensional irreducible module with xv_i=i v_i and yv_i=v_(i+1) cyclically, so it has no common eigenline.
items.strategy: Check [rho(x),rho(y)]=rho(y). An invariant subspace stable under x is spanned by selected distinct weight vectors, and cyclic y-stability forces all of them, proving irreducibility.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Remark 13.2

items.title: Engel's theorem for strictly upper triangular matrices
items.statement: For n_n acting on k^n, every element is nilpotent, e_1 is a common zero vector in the standard upper-triangular convention, and the standard flag realizes Engel triangularization.
items.strategy: Compute the action on standard basis vectors and identify the invariant flag and common kernel explicitly.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 2.8 and n(F) example

title: Semisimple Lie Algebras Cohomology and Levi Theory

items.title: Simple, semisimple, and reductive Lie algebras
items.statement: A simple Lie algebra is nonabelian and has no ideals except 0 and itself. Semisimple means zero radical. In characteristic zero, reductive means a direct sum of its center and a semisimple derived algebra.
items.strategy: Consolidate the standing conventions, explicitly excluding one-dimensional abelian algebras from simple and allowing the zero algebra to be semisimple.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §§4 and 6

items.title: Trace form of a representation
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional representation rho:g→gl(V), define B_rho(x,y)=tr(rho(x)rho(y)).
items.strategy: Use the basis-independent trace of an endomorphism; finite dimensionality of V is essential.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §6.1

items.title: Killing form
items.statement: The Killing form of finite-dimensional g is K_g(x,y)=tr(ad_x ad_y), the trace form of the adjoint representation.
items.strategy: Specialize the trace-form construction to ad and keep the base-field and finite-dimensional hypotheses explicit.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §4, Killing form

items.title: Trace forms are symmetric and invariant
items.statement: B_rho is bilinear, symmetric, and invariant: B_rho([z,x],y)+B_rho(x,[z,y])=0. Hence the Killing form has these properties.
items.strategy: Use tr(AB)=tr(BA) for symmetry and expand rho([z,x]) as a commutator; cyclically move factors until the two invariant terms cancel.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Lemma 6.1

items.title: Orthogonal complements under invariant forms are ideals
items.statement: If B is a symmetric invariant bilinear form on g and i is an ideal, then i^perp is an ideal. In particular ker(B)=g^perp is an ideal.
items.strategy: For x in i^perp, z in g, and y in i, invariance gives B([z,x],y)=-B(x,[z,y])=0 because [z,y] lies in i.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Proposition 14.12

items.title: Cartan's solvability criterion
items.statement: Let g be finite-dimensional over a characteristic-zero field. Then g is solvable iff K_g(g,[g,g])=0. More generally, a finite-dimensional linear Lie algebra h⊆gl(V) is solvable if tr(xy)=0 for every x in [h,h] and y in h.
items.strategy: After scalar extension, Lie triangularization proves necessity. For sufficiency, for x in [h,h] use polynomial Jordan decomposition and the trace pairing with the semisimple part of x to show that part is zero; Engel then makes [h,h] nilpotent. Apply this linear criterion to ad(g), and use the solvable-extension result for 0→Z(g)→g→ad(g)→0.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorems 3.17–3.18

items.title: Cartan's semisimplicity criterion
items.statement: A finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field is semisimple iff its Killing form is nondegenerate.
items.strategy: If g is semisimple, the Killing radical is an ideal and its intrinsic Killing form vanishes, so Cartan's criterion makes it solvable and hence zero. Conversely every abelian ideal a is Killing-orthogonal to g because (ad_a ad_g)^2=0; nondegeneracy forces a=0. The last nonzero derived term of any nonzero solvable ideal would be a nonzero abelian ideal, so the radical vanishes.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 1.45

items.title: Semisimple Lie algebras are centerless and perfect
items.statement: If g is semisimple in characteristic zero, then Z(g)=0 and [g,g]=g.
items.strategy: The center lies in the Killing radical, so it vanishes. The quotient g/[g,g] is abelian; its inverse image would enlarge the radical unless the quotient is zero.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Corollary 15.5

items.title: Semisimple Lie algebras decompose into simple ideals
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field is a finite direct sum of simple ideals.
items.strategy: Choose a nonzero ideal minimal by finite dimension. Nondegeneracy and the orthogonal-complement lemma split it from its complement; show the restriction is nondegenerate and induct on dimension. Minimal nonabelian ideals are simple, since an abelian minimal ideal would be solvable.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, structure theorem in §4

items.title: Ideals and quotients of semisimple Lie algebras
items.statement: Every ideal and quotient of a finite-dimensional semisimple characteristic-zero Lie algebra is semisimple; each ideal is the sum of a subfamily of the simple ideals and has an ideal complement.
items.strategy: Project an ideal to each simple summand; bracketing with that summand shows a nonzero projection forces inclusion of the whole summand. Read both the ideal and quotient as complementary direct sums.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Theorem 15.3 and Corollary 15.7

items.title: Casimir operator relative to an invariant form
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional g with nondegenerate invariant symmetric form B and dual bases (x_i),(x^i), define Omega_B=sum_i x_i x^i in U(g); on a representation V its action is sum_i rho(x_i)rho(x^i).
items.strategy: Use nondegeneracy to obtain the dual basis and the enveloping-algebra product; independence and centrality are supplied by the next lemma.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §7.8.8

items.title: The Casimir operator is basis-independent and intertwining
items.statement: Omega_B is independent of the dual basis, commutes with g in U(g), and therefore acts as a g-intertwiner on every representation.
items.strategy: Identify sum_i x_i tensor x^i with the inverse tensor of B, hence basis-independent. Invariance of B makes this tensor diagonal-adjoint invariant; applying multiplication in U(g) shows [x,Omega_B]=0.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §6.3

items.title: Weyl's complete reducibility theorem
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional representation of a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over any characteristic-zero field is completely reducible.
items.strategy: Over an algebraic closure, use a minimal nonsplit submodule extension and the Casimir constructed from the nondegenerate trace form of the image to obtain an invariant projection, contradicting minimality. Descend the solution of the finite linear system defining an invariant complement to the base field.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 5.20

items.title: Equivalent characterizations of reductive Lie algebras
items.statement: For finite-dimensional g in characteristic zero, the following are equivalent: rad(g)=Z(g); g=Z(g)⊕[g,g] with [g,g] semisimple; and the adjoint representation is completely reducible.
items.strategy: If rad(g)=Z(g), let the semisimple quotient act on g through adjoints and use Weyl to split the central submodule; the complement is an ideal mapping isomorphically to the quotient and equals [g,g]. The direct-sum form and Weyl give complete reducibility. Conversely, split the radical and then its derived ideal as adjoint submodules. Complementary ideals commute, forcing the solvable derived ideal to be perfect and therefore zero; the resulting abelian radical commutes with its ideal complement and is central.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Proposition 6.2

items.title: The adjoint representation splits into simple ideals
items.statement: For semisimple g, every adjoint submodule is an ideal with an ideal complement; the irreducible adjoint summands are precisely simple ideals.
items.strategy: Apply Weyl to ad(g), translate invariant subspaces into ideals, and compare with the simple-ideal decomposition.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Theorem 15.3

items.title: Derivations of semisimple Lie algebras are inner
items.statement: For finite-dimensional semisimple g in characteristic zero, Der(g)=ad(g), uniquely because Z(g)=0.
items.strategy: Extend the Killing form from ad(g) to Der(g) by tr_g(DE). Split off the nondegenerate ideal ad(g) by its orthogonal complement; an orthogonal derivation commutes with every ad_x, hence ad_(Dx)=0 and centerlessness gives D=0.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Proposition 15.8

items.title: Lie algebra of the automorphism group
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. For a finite-dimensional real or complex semisimple Lie algebra g, Aut(g) is a closed Lie subgroup of GL(g) and Lie(Aut(g))=Der(g)=ad(g).
items.strategy: Express bracket preservation as closed polynomial equations and invoke the published closed-subgroup theorem, whose construction is the exact use of AC_omega. Differentiate A[x,y]=[Ax,Ay] at the identity to obtain the derivation law, and use the inner-derivation theorem.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Corollary 15.9

items.title: Chevalley–Eilenberg cochains
items.statement: For a Lie algebra g and g-module M, define C^n(g,M)=Hom_k(Λ^n g,M) for n>=0 and C^n=0 for n<0, with C^0=M.
items.strategy: Use the published arbitrary-field exterior power and Hom space; finite dimensionality is not needed for this definition.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §7.7

items.title: Chevalley–Eilenberg differential
items.statement: For f in C^n, define (df)(x_0,...,x_n)=sum_i(-1)^i x_i f(x_0,...,hat{x_i},...,x_n)+sum_(i<j)(-1)^(i+j) f([x_i,x_j],x_0,...,hat{x_i},...,hat{x_j},...,x_n).
items.strategy: Fix the zero-based sign convention explicitly; alternation makes the formula factor through Λ^(n+1)g, and d squared is justified next.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §7.7.1–7.7.3

items.title: The Chevalley–Eilenberg differential squares to zero
items.statement: For every n and every f in C^n(g,M), d^(n+1)d^n f=0.
items.strategy: Expand d(df) and group terms: double action terms pair to rho([x_i,x_j]); these cancel the terms where the outer differential acts on the inner bracket. Terms with two disjoint brackets cancel in opposite orders, and the three nested-bracket terms for each triple cancel by Jacobi with the declared signs. This is a direct proof, not an appeal to the name of the complex.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, Exercise 7.7.1 and surrounding differential

items.title: Lie algebra cohomology
items.statement: The cohomology of the Chevalley–Eilenberg cochain complex is H^n(g,M)=ker(d:C^n→C^(n+1))/im(d:C^(n-1)→C^n).
items.strategy: Apply the published cochain-complex and cohomology construction after d squared zero; retain the same cohomological grading convention.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, Corollary 7.7.3

items.title: Zeroth Lie algebra cohomology is invariants
items.statement: H^0(g,M)=M^g={m:xm=0 for all x in g}.
items.strategy: Compute d^0(m)(x)=xm and note there are no degree-minus-one coboundaries.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, §47.1

items.title: First cohomology is derivations modulo inner derivations
items.statement: A 1-cocycle delta:g→M satisfies delta([x,y])=x delta(y)-y delta(x), and 1-coboundaries are delta_m(x)=xm. Thus H^1(g,M)=Der(g,M)/Inn(g,M); for M=g this is Der(g)/ad(g).
items.strategy: Evaluate the declared differential in degrees zero and one and identify its kernel and image with the module-valued derivation and inner-derivation formulas.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §7.4.3–7.4.4

items.title: Second cohomology classifies abelian extensions
items.statement: For a finite-dimensional Lie algebra g and a fixed g-module M, H^2(g,M) bijects with equivalence classes of extensions 0→M→e→g→0 inducing the given action and having M abelian. The zero class corresponds exactly to split extensions.
items.strategy: Choose a section by lifting a finite basis of g and measure its bracket defect omega. Jacobi is exactly d omega=0; changing the section adds a coboundary. Conversely put the cocycle-twisted bracket on M⊕g, check Jacobi, and verify these constructions and equivalences are inverse.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §7.6 and Exercise 7.7.5

items.title: First Whitehead lemma
items.statement: If g is finite-dimensional semisimple over a characteristic-zero field and M is a finite-dimensional g-module, then H^1(g,M)=0.
items.strategy: Given a cocycle delta, put the g-module structure x·(m,a)=(xm+a delta(x),0) on M⊕k. Weyl supplies an invariant complement to M; a generator (m,1) of that complement is invariant, so delta(x)=-xm is a coboundary.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, Theorem 7.8.9 and Corollary 7.8.10

items.title: Second Whitehead lemma
items.statement: If g is finite-dimensional semisimple over a characteristic-zero field and M is a finite-dimensional g-module, then H^2(g,M)=0.
items.strategy: For a nontrivial simple module, use the standard Chevalley–Eilenberg contraction homotopy for the Casimir: its action on positive cohomology is both zero and a nonzero scalar, so H^2 vanishes. Weyl reduces M to simple summands. For the trivial simple module, classify a central extension, let g act on its middle algebra by lifted adjoints, split the projection by Weyl, and observe that the module section is a Lie section.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, Corollary 7.8.12

items.title: Long exact sequence in Lie algebra cohomology
items.statement: For finite-dimensional g and a short exact sequence 0→M'→M→M''→0 of g-modules, the induced sequence of Chevalley–Eilenberg complexes is degreewise short exact and yields the natural long exact sequence ...→H^n(g,M')→H^n(g,M)→H^n(g,M'')→H^(n+1)(g,M')→....
items.strategy: Because Λ^n g is finite-dimensional, Hom_k(Λ^n g,-) preserves the short exact sequence: choose a finite basis to lift maps. Check the maps commute with the CE differential, then invoke the published cohomology long exact sequence with its degree-raising connecting map.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §§7.7–7.8

items.title: Levi subalgebras and Levi decompositions
items.statement: A Levi subalgebra s of g is a semisimple subalgebra complementary to rad(g) as a vector space; the canonical map from the acting-algebra-first product s⋉rad(g) to g is an isomorphism, called a Levi decomposition.
items.strategy: Use the cited acting-algebra-first semidirect-product convention and do not assert existence or uniqueness in the definition.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Definition 6.24

items.title: Levi decomposition theorem
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field has a Levi subalgebra, so g=rad(g)⋊s with s congruent to g/rad(g).
items.strategy: Induct on the derived length of the radical r. If r is abelian, the extension class in H^2(g/r,r) vanishes and gives a section. Otherwise quotient by [r,r], split there, and let h be the inverse image of that quotient Levi factor; rad(h)=[r,r], whose derived length is smaller, so induction inside h supplies the required Levi factor.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, Levi's Theorem 7.8.13

items.title: Malcev conjugacy of Levi subalgebras
items.statement: Any two Levi subalgebras of a finite-dimensional characteristic-zero g are conjugate by a finite product of automorphisms exp(ad x) with x in nilrad(g).
items.strategy: Strengthen the claim by placing every conjugator in [g,rad(g)] and induct on dim rad(g). If [g,rad(g)]=0, perfectness makes the Levi section unique. Otherwise choose a minimal g-ideal m in the nonzero center of the nilpotent ideal [g,rad(g)]. The minimal-radical case is a Whitehead-I cocycle graph; in the general case the strengthened quotient conjugators lift from [g/m,rad(g)/m]=[g,rad(g)]/m, and one final cocycle graph with values in m completes the conjugation.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 6.25

items.title: Levi factors are noncanonical but conjugate
items.statement: Levi factors need not be equal, but all are isomorphic to g/rad(g) and are conjugate by inner unipotent automorphisms generated from the nilradical.
items.strategy: Combine projection isomorphisms with Malcev conjugacy, then exhibit two distinct factors in the standard semidirect product sl_2⋉k^2.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 6.25

items.title: Ado's theorem with nilpotent nilradical action
items.statement: For finite-dimensional g over a characteristic-zero field, there is a finite-dimensional faithful representation rho such that rho(x) is nilpotent for every x in nilrad(g).
items.strategy: Follow Knapp's Zassenhaus construction: start from a faithful representation of a solvable ideal with nilpotent nilradical action; in U(h), stabilize a finite-codimensional ideal under the required derivations and represent the semidirect extension on the finite quotient. Induct on solvable algebras, then extend across a Levi factor and add its adjoint representation. Over a general characteristic-zero field, construct over the algebraic closure, descend the finitely many matrix coefficients to a finite extension, and restrict scalars.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Appendix B, Theorems B.9–B.12

items.title: Every finite-dimensional characteristic-zero Lie algebra is a matrix Lie algebra
items.statement: Every finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a characteristic-zero field is isomorphic to a Lie subalgebra of gl_n(k) for some finite n.
items.strategy: Take Ado's faithful representation and identify g with its image using the Lie-algebra first isomorphism theorem.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem B.8

items.title: Lie's second fundamental theorem
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. If G is a connected simply connected real Lie group and H a real Lie group, every Lie-algebra homomorphism Lie(G)→Lie(H) integrates to a unique smooth Lie-group homomorphism G→H.
items.strategy: Integrate the graph Lie subalgebra inside G×H. Projection of its connected immersed subgroup to G is a local diffeomorphism and covering; simple connectivity makes it an isomorphism, producing the homomorphism. Uniqueness follows because equal differentials give equal graphs (or by lift uniqueness). AC_omega is used exactly by the published subgroup–subalgebra correspondence's maximal-leaf construction.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Theorem 3.38

items.title: Lie's third fundamental theorem
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. Every finite-dimensional real Lie algebra is the Lie algebra of a connected simply connected real Lie group, unique up to Lie-group isomorphism.
items.strategy: Use Ado to embed g in gl_n(R), integrate it to a connected immersed subgroup of GL_n(R), and take that subgroup's universal covering Lie group. Covering differentials preserve the Lie algebra. For uniqueness, integrate an algebra isomorphism and its inverse by Lie II and use uniqueness there to make their composites identities. AC_omega enters only through the subgroup-integration and Lie II theorems; the Ado and covering arguments introduce no stronger choice.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem B.7

items.title: Equivalence of simply connected Lie groups and real Lie algebras
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. The Lie functor from connected simply connected real Lie groups to finite-dimensional real Lie algebras is an equivalence of categories.
items.strategy: Lie III supplies essential surjectivity. Lie II supplies fullness and uniqueness supplies faithfulness; verify composition and identities by their differentials.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, Corollary 3.39

items.title: Connected Lie groups are central quotients of simply connected integrations
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. Every connected real Lie group G is isomorphic to G_tilde/Gamma, where G_tilde is its simply connected covering Lie group and Gamma is a discrete central subgroup; conversely each such quotient has the same Lie algebra.
items.strategy: The kernel of the covering homomorphism is discrete and normal. For fixed gamma, the conjugacy map from connected G_tilde to the discrete kernel is constant, so gamma is central. Apply the Lie-group first-isomorphism factorization and local-diffeomorphism property. AC_omega is inherited exactly through the published discrete-subgroup theorem used for Gamma.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §3.8

items.title: Exponential diffeomorphism for simply connected nilpotent Lie groups
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. If N is a connected simply connected real Lie group with nilpotent Lie algebra n, then exp:n→N is a diffeomorphism. In these coordinates multiplication is the BCH polynomial, which terminates after finitely many bracket lengths.
items.strategy: Use truncated BCH to put a polynomial group law on the vector space n; local associativity globalizes because the associator is polynomial and vanishes on an open set. This BCH group is simply connected and has exponential equal to the identity. Lie II integrates the identity Lie-algebra map in both directions between it and N, and uniqueness makes the maps inverse. AC_omega is inherited through BCH, the exponential supplier, and Lie II.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 1.127

items.title: Connected nilpotent Lie groups are central quotients of BCH groups
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. Every connected real Lie group with nilpotent Lie algebra is a quotient of the BCH group on that algebra by a discrete central subgroup.
items.strategy: Identify the simply connected cover with the BCH group by the exponential diffeomorphism, then apply the central-quotient theorem.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 1.127 and Corollary 1.134

items.title: Lie algebras determine connected Lie groups only locally
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. Connected real Lie groups with isomorphic Lie algebras have isomorphic identity neighborhoods as local Lie groups, but may differ globally through distinct discrete central quotients of the same simply connected integration.
items.strategy: Lift both groups to the unique simply connected integration, identify the covers via Lie II/III, and compare their possibly different discrete central kernels; local covering charts give the local isomorphism.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §3.8

items.title: Centerless implies semisimple
items.statement: False: a centerless finite-dimensional Lie algebra can have nonzero solvable radical.
items.strategy: Use the two-dimensional affine algebra [x,y]=y: its center is zero, but it is solvable and nonzero, so its radical is all of it.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §§3–4 (proper radical definition)

items.title: The Killing form is nondegenerate on every reductive Lie algebra
items.statement: False: the Killing form of a reductive algebra is degenerate when its center is nonzero.
items.strategy: Every central element has zero adjoint action; use gl_n or a nonzero abelian algebra as an explicit reductive example.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §6.1

items.title: Every finite-dimensional representation of a reductive Lie algebra is completely reducible
items.statement: False: Weyl's theorem applies to semisimple algebras; a reductive center may act nonsemisimply.
items.strategy: Let a one-dimensional abelian algebra act on k^2 by a nonzero nilpotent Jordan block. Its invariant line has no invariant complement.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 6.14

items.title: Second cohomology classifies all nonabelian extensions
items.statement: False: H^2(g,M) classifies extensions only when the kernel is abelian and the induced g-module structure on it is fixed.
items.strategy: Point to the Jacobi calculation, which uses the abelian-kernel bracket; nonabelian kernels also require outer-action and nonabelian obstruction data.

references.title: Weibel, Lie Algebra Homology and Cohomology, §7.6

items.title: Levi subalgebras are literally unique
items.statement: False: Levi subalgebras are generally conjugate, not equal.
items.strategy: Use a semidirect product s⋉V with a nontrivial coboundary: conjugation by exp(ad v) moves the standard Levi complement to a distinct one.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, Theorem 6.25

items.title: Isomorphic Lie algebras determine isomorphic connected Lie groups
items.statement: Assume AC_omega. False: distinct discrete central quotients of one simply connected Lie group have the same Lie algebra.
items.strategy: Use R and S^1, or SU(2) and SO(3), and distinguish the groups by compactness or fundamental group.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §3.8

title: Semisimple Lie Algebras Cohomology and Levi Theory — Examples

items.title: Killing form of sl_2
items.statement: For the standard basis e,f,h of sl_2 with [h,e]=2e, [h,f]=-2f, [e,f]=h, the Killing form has K(h,h)=8, K(e,f)=4, and all other basis pairings forced by symmetry are zero; it is nondegenerate in characteristic zero.
items.strategy: Write the three adjoint matrices, multiply, take traces, and compute the determinant of the Gram matrix.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Ch. I examples after Cartan's criterion

items.title: Classical simple Lie algebras and their Killing forms
items.statement: For the split classical matrix algebras over characteristic zero, K_sl_n(X,Y)=2n tr(XY) for n>=2, K_so_n(X,Y)=(n-2)tr(XY) for n=3 or n>=5, and K_sp_(2n)(X,Y)=2(n+1)tr(XY) for n>=1. In these simple ranges the forms are nondegenerate; the low-rank orthogonal exceptions are stated separately.
items.strategy: Evaluate ad on matrix units and use invariance to reduce to diagonal and root-vector pairings; state the low-rank exceptions separately rather than calling every member simple.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Ch. I §§7–8

items.title: A reductive algebra with degenerate Killing form
items.statement: For n>=1, gl_n in characteristic zero is reductive with decomposition kI⊕sl_n, but its Killing form vanishes on the central line kI and is therefore degenerate.
items.strategy: Identify the center and derived algebra, then note ad_I=0.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Example 14.14

items.title: Direct-sum decomposition of a semisimple Lie algebra
items.statement: For g=sl_2⊕sl_3, the two summands are simple ideals, every ideal is the sum of a subcollection of them, and the Killing form is their orthogonal direct sum.
items.strategy: Compute componentwise brackets and adjoints, then apply the ideal classification to the two nonisomorphic simple factors.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Proposition 15.6

items.title: First cohomology with trivial coefficients
items.statement: For the trivial module k, H^1(g,k) is naturally (g/[g,g])^*.
items.strategy: The cocycle equation becomes lambda([x,y])=0 and all degree-one coboundaries vanish; factor linear forms through the abelianization.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, §47.1

items.title: The Heisenberg algebra from a two-cocycle
items.statement: For the two-dimensional abelian g with trivial one-dimensional module k, the alternating form omega(x,y)=1 is a 2-cocycle whose extension is the Heisenberg algebra.
items.strategy: The CE differential is zero in the needed degrees; insert omega into the twisted bracket and obtain [x,y]=z with z central.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Example 47.4

items.title: A Levi decomposition of the Euclidean-motion algebra of R^3
items.statement: For the Euclidean-motion algebra of three-space e(3)=R^3⋊so(3), the translation ideal R^3 is the radical and so(3) is a Levi factor.
items.strategy: The quotient by translations is semisimple, translations are abelian, and any solvable ideal projects trivially to the simple quotient; verify the displayed complement.

references.title: Etingof, Lie Groups and Lie Algebras notes, Example 14.8

items.title: Distinct conjugate Levi subalgebras
items.statement: In g=sl_2⋉V for a finite-dimensional module V with nontrivial action, the standard sl_2 and exp(ad v)(sl_2) are distinct Levi subalgebras for suitable v in V, yet are Malcev-conjugate.
items.strategy: Because V is abelian, exp(ad v)=1+ad v. Choose v not invariant; then x maps to x-[x,v], producing a different graph complement with the same projection.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, proof of Theorem 6.25

items.title: SU(2) and SO(3): same local Lie theory, different groups
items.statement: The covering homomorphism SU(2)→SO(3) has kernel {±I}, induces su(2) congruent to so(3), and makes the groups locally isomorphic, but SU(2) is simply connected while SO(3) has fundamental group Z/2.
items.strategy: Use conjugation on imaginary quaternions for the double cover, compute the differential, and distinguish the groups by their covering kernels.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §3.8 examples

items.title: The BCH group of a nilpotent Lie algebra
items.statement: On a finite-dimensional real nilpotent Lie algebra n, x*y=BCH(x,y) is a finite polynomial group law with identity 0 and inverse -x; its Lie algebra is n and it is connected and simply connected.
items.strategy: Nilpotence truncates BCH. Associativity follows first locally from the BCH theorem and then globally because both sides are polynomial identities; the underlying manifold is the vector space.

references.title: Knapp, Lie Groups Beyond an Introduction, Theorem 1.127

items.title: Centerless does not imply semisimple
items.statement: The nonabelian two-dimensional affine Lie algebra is centerless but solvable, hence not semisimple.
items.strategy: Solve [ax+by,x]=[ax+by,y]=0 to get a=b=0 and use its earlier derived-series computation.

references.title: Milne, Lie Algebras, §§3–4

items.title: The circle and line have the same Lie algebra but different Lie groups
items.statement: The connected Lie groups (R,+) and S^1 have isomorphic one-dimensional abelian Lie algebras, but are not isomorphic because S^1 is compact and R is not.
items.strategy: Compute both brackets as zero and use compactness, preserved by any Lie-group isomorphism, to separate the groups.

references.title: Kirillov, An Introduction to Lie Groups and Lie Algebras, §3.8
